notes: The whole arc of a working life in music, from the first pulse to the royalty statement: the sound, the song, the room, the studio and the industry. Every block ends in something made or done on real material — a played phrase, a written verse, a mixed track, a costed gig. Louisiana's own grooves and its own music economy are the ground. Stance: practising a craft here is not a union card, a license or a contract; the American Federation of Musicians, the performing-rights organisations and the courts are the front doors for those, and this pack teaches how to walk up to them.

tracks.name: The sound: instrument, voice and ear

themes.description: Beat, subdivision and the second-line clap: feeling time in the body before counting it, and the Louisiana habit of putting the accent where the street puts it.
themes.transfer_check: Keep steady time with a metronome at three tempos while clapping the second-line pattern, then recorded and self-checked against the click.

bands.K–2: Clap along to a song with an adult and find the steady beat.
bands.3–5: Clap a steady beat to three different songs and say which was fastest.
bands.6–8: Clap a beat and its subdivision together for one song, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Clap a beat and its subdivision together for one real song, and say where the accent falls.
bands.11–12: Lead a group in clapping a real song's pulse and subdivision, and defend where the accent falls and why.

themes.theme: The voice as the first instrument
themes.description: Breath, pitch-matching and the speaking voice turned into the singing voice; care of the instrument you were born with.
themes.transfer_check: Match twelve played pitches by voice within a semitone, recorded, and sing a four-line melody in tune with a drone.

bands.K–2: Sing a note back to an adult as closely as you can match it.
bands.3–5: Match pitch to three notes played for you and say which was hardest.
bands.6–8: Match pitch on five notes and describe one thing that helps breath support, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Match pitch on five real notes and describe one habit that protects your speaking and singing voice.
bands.11–12: Match pitch reliably across a real range and teach a beginner one habit that protects the voice.

themes.description: A first real instrument — guitar, keyboard, horn, accordion, drum — its parts, its care, and the first ten notes played cleanly.
themes.transfer_check: Play a one-octave scale and a four-bar phrase cleanly on a real instrument, and demonstrate tuning and basic maintenance on it.

bands.K–2: Hold a real instrument with an adult and play one clean note.
bands.3–5: Play three clean notes on a real instrument and name one part of it.
bands.6–8: Play ten clean notes on a real instrument and name its parts, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Play the first ten notes of a real instrument cleanly and explain how you care for it.
bands.11–12: Play a real instrument's first ten notes cleanly for an audience and explain its care and its parts.

themes.description: Training the ear to name what it hears: intervals, major and minor, the I–IV–V that most songs live on.
themes.transfer_check: Identify by ear eight intervals and six chord qualities played at random, scoring at least three in four.

bands.K–2: Say whether two notes played together sound happy or sad.
bands.3–5: Tell apart a major and a minor chord played for you.
bands.6–8: Name three intervals played for you and say if a chord is major or minor, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Name three real intervals by ear and identify a I–IV–V progression in a real song.
bands.11–12: Identify intervals and a I–IV–V progression by ear in a real song, and teach the trick to someone else.

themes.description: Notation, tablature, chord charts and the Nashville numbers — and the ear-first tradition that built jazz and zydeco without them.
themes.transfer_check: Read a lead sheet well enough to play its melody and chords, and learn a second tune entirely by ear from a recording.

bands.K–2: Follow a simple picture of a song's shape with an adult while it plays.
bands.3–5: Follow a chord chart for one real song while it plays.
bands.6–8: Read a simple chord chart for one real song and play along, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Read a real chord chart or tab for one song and play along, and explain what the ear-first tradition does instead.
bands.11–12: Read and play from a real chart, and explain to a beginner why ear-first traditions built whole genres without one.

themes.description: Second line, the zydeco two-step, the Cajun waltz, swamp pop and bounce: what makes each one itself, felt in the feet and the hands.
themes.transfer_check: Play or clap four distinct Louisiana grooves at correct feel and tempo, naming what distinguishes each, for a listener who can tell the difference.

bands.K–2: Move your feet to a Louisiana rhythm with an adult and say how it feels.
bands.3–5: Move to three real Louisiana grooves and say which is which.
bands.6–8: Identify three real Louisiana grooves by ear and clap one, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Identify three real Louisiana grooves by ear and clap the pattern that makes one of them itself.
bands.11–12: Identify and demonstrate a real Louisiana groove for an audience, and explain what makes it itself.

themes.description: Listening, locking to the drummer, leaving space and passing the lead — the ensemble skills no solo practice teaches.
themes.transfer_check: Hold a part in a three-person ensemble through a full tune without dropping time, then trade a four-bar solo with another player.

bands.K–2: Take turns playing one note each with a friend, in time.
bands.3–5: Play a simple pattern with a partner without rushing or slowing down.
bands.6–8: Play a simple part with a partner and leave space for their lead, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Play a real part with a partner, locking to their time and leaving space for their lead.
bands.11–12: Play a real ensemble part, listening across the group and passing the lead cleanly at least once.

themes.description: The loop, the slow-down, the metronome and the log: getting better on purpose instead of by accident.
themes.transfer_check: Keep a two-week practice log with a target phrase, and demonstrate it at a tempo 20% faster than on day one.

bands.K–2: Practise one short phrase five times in a row with an adult watching.
bands.3–5: Practise a short phrase with a metronome and say if it got easier.
bands.6–8: Practise one phrase with a metronome and log what changed, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Practise a real phrase with a metronome and a log, and show what changed over a week.
bands.11–12: Run a real week-long practice log with a metronome and slow-down technique, and show the measured improvement.

themes.description: Tuning systems, strings, reeds, mouthpieces, the accordion's bellows and the electric signal: knowing the machine you play.
themes.transfer_check: Change strings or a reed (or service an accordion bellows or a drum head) and return the instrument to playing pitch.

bands.K–2: Look at how your instrument makes a sound with an adult and name one part.
bands.3–5: Tune a real instrument with help and say what tuning means.
bands.6–8: Tune a real instrument by yourself and name one part that shapes its sound, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Tune a real instrument and explain one part of its technology that shapes tone.
bands.11–12: Tune and explain a real instrument's technology — strings, reeds or signal — to someone new to it.

themes.theme: Protecting the ear and the body
themes.description: Hearing loss is permanent; repetitive strain is real. Earplugs, posture, breaks, and the musician's long body.
themes.transfer_check: Measure a rehearsal's sound level with a phone meter, choose protection for it, and demonstrate a posture and warm-up routine for your instrument.

bands.K–2: Say why loud sound can hurt your ears, and use ear protection with an adult.
bands.3–5: Say one habit that protects a musician's ears or body.
bands.6–8: Name two habits that protect a musician's hearing and body, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Name two real habits that protect a musician's hearing and body, and use one during practice.
bands.11–12: Design and follow a real hearing and body-care routine for a musician, and teach it to a bandmate.

themes.description: The hook, the title and the line you cannot shake: catching an idea and keeping it before it leaves.
themes.transfer_check: Collect twenty song ideas in a week — titles, lines, hummed phrases — and develop one into a hook with a recorded eight bars.

bands.K–2: Say one idea you would put in a song, with an adult helping.
bands.3–5: Write down one line or title you cannot stop thinking about.
bands.6–8: Catch one song idea and keep it in a notebook before it leaves, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Catch a real song idea — a hook or title — and hold it in a notebook before it leaves.
bands.11–12: Catch and develop a real idea into a working title or hook, and defend why it is worth keeping.

themes.description: Rhyme, meter, the concrete image over the vague feeling, and the first line's job of earning the second.
themes.transfer_check: Write a verse and chorus with a consistent meter and a concrete image in every line, then revise it after reading it aloud to someone.

bands.K–2: Make two words rhyme together, with an adult helping you find them.
bands.3–5: Write two lines that rhyme about something you saw today.
bands.6–8: Write four lines using rhyme and one concrete image, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write four real lines using rhyme, meter and a concrete image instead of a vague feeling.
bands.11–12: Write a real verse where the first line earns the second, using rhyme, meter and concrete image throughout.

themes.description: Writing a tune that moves: contour, range, repetition with variation, and a melody a stranger can sing back.
themes.transfer_check: Write a melody over a given four-chord progression that a listener can sing back after two hearings.

bands.K–2: Hum a simple tune with an adult that goes up and down.
bands.3–5: Hum a short tune over a simple chord and see if a friend can sing it back.
bands.6–8: Write a short melody over a chord and have someone sing it back, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write a real melody over changes and have a stranger sing it back after one hearing.
bands.11–12: Write and test a real melody's contour and repetition, refined until a stranger sings it back accurately.

themes.description: The three chords, the fourth one, the borrowed chord and the turnaround — how harmony colours a line.
themes.transfer_check: Reharmonise a simple melody two ways and explain, on the instrument, what each change does to the feeling.

bands.K–2: Play two chords with an adult and say which sounds more like an ending.
bands.3–5: Play three chords in a row and say which one feels like a turn.
bands.6–8: Play four chords including a borrowed one and say what it changes, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Play a real progression with a borrowed chord and explain what colour it adds to the line.
bands.11–12: Choose and defend a real harmony including a turnaround, explaining what each chord does to the song.

themes.description: Verse, chorus, bridge; the 12-bar blues; the jazz head and the AABA — the shapes songs come in and why.
themes.transfer_check: Map the form of three recorded songs from different Louisiana genres and write an original song in one of those forms.

bands.K–2: Say which part of a song repeats: the chorus.
bands.3–5: Label the verse and chorus of a real song.
bands.6–8: Label verse, chorus and bridge in a real song, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Label a real song's full form — verse, chorus, bridge — and say why it is shaped that way.
bands.11–12: Analyse a real song's form against a named shape (12-bar, AABA) and defend the match.

themes.description: Who plays what, when to stop, the intro and the ending — turning a song into a piece a band can play.
themes.transfer_check: Write a one-page arrangement (intro, sections, dynamics, ending) for a four-piece band and rehearse it with them once.

bands.K–2: Say who plays first and who plays last in a simple group song.
bands.3–5: Decide with a group who plays what for one simple song.
bands.6–8: Arrange one song for three instruments, deciding who plays what, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Arrange a real song for a small band, deciding the intro, the ending and who plays what.
bands.11–12: Arrange and rehearse a real song for a band, with a written chart and a defended ending.

themes.theme: The horn section and the rhythm section
themes.description: Writing parts: a horn line that fits the vocal, a bass line that locks to the kick, a keyboard part that leaves room.
themes.transfer_check: Write and notate or chart a two-horn line and a bass part for an existing song, and hear them played by real players.

bands.K–2: Say which instrument keeps the beat in a band.
bands.3–5: Point out the bass and the drums doing their jobs in a real song.
bands.6–8: Write a simple bass line that locks to the drum in one song, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write a real bass line that locks to the kick and a keyboard part that leaves room.
bands.11–12: Write real horn and rhythm parts that fit together, and have a band play them as written.

themes.description: Two people in a room: the split, the credit, and the habits that make collaboration work instead of end.
themes.transfer_check: Co-write a complete song with a partner, agree the split in writing before finishing, and each perform the other's contribution.

bands.K–2: Write one line of a song with a friend, taking turns.
bands.3–5: Write half a song with a partner and agree who did what.
bands.6–8: Co-write four lines with a partner and agree the split, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Co-write a real verse with a partner, agreeing the split and the credit in writing.
bands.11–12: Co-write a real song with a partner through to finish, with a written split-sheet habit that made it work.

themes.description: The phone, the sketch and the honest rough: a demo that shows the song, not the production.
themes.transfer_check: Record a clear voice-and-instrument demo of an original song, under three minutes, that a stranger can understand on one listen.

bands.K–2: Record yourself singing a short line on a phone with an adult.
bands.3–5: Record a rough phone demo of one song idea.
bands.6–8: Record a phone demo of one song that shows the idea, not polish, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Record a real phone demo of one song that shows the song, not the production.
bands.11–12: Record and share a real honest demo of a finished song, defended as showing the song rather than the polish.

themes.description: What you own the moment a song is fixed, what registration adds, and what a split sheet is for.
themes.transfer_check: Fill in a split sheet for a co-written song and complete a copyright-registration form correctly (submission optional and at the writer's choice).

bands.K–2: Say that the moment you make up a song, it is yours.
bands.3–5: Say what it means that a song is yours the moment you write it down.
bands.6–8: State what you own the moment a song is fixed and what a split sheet is for, with a checker.
bands.9–10: State what you own the moment a song is fixed, what registration adds, and complete a split sheet.
bands.11–12: Complete a real split sheet for a co-written song and explain to the co-writer what each protection means.

themes.description: Building an hour: opener, the lull, the peak, the encore; keys and tempos that flow; the song you cut.
themes.transfer_check: Build and play a forty-five-minute set list with written reasoning for its order, then revise it after one performance.

bands.K–2: Pick which song to play first and which to play last, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Put three songs in an order that starts strong and ends strong.
bands.6–8: Order five songs into an opener, a peak and an encore, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Order a real set of songs into an opener, a peak and an encore, and say which song you cut and why.
bands.11–12: Build and defend a real hour-long set list with keys and tempos that flow, cutting one song on purpose.

themes.description: The stage plot, the input list and the monitor mix: getting the sound right before the door opens.
themes.transfer_check: Produce a stage plot and input list for your act and run a sound check with a sound engineer using them.

bands.K–2: Say your name into a microphone with an adult before a show.
bands.3–5: Check that each instrument can be heard before a small performance.
bands.6–8: Write a simple stage plot for one band and check each input, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write a real stage plot and input list, and get the monitor mix right before doors.
bands.11–12: Run a real sound check from stage plot to monitor mix, and get the room ready before doors open.

themes.theme: The front line and the back line
themes.description: Stage roles: who leads, who cues, who counts in; the bandleader's hand and the sideman's ear.
themes.transfer_check: Lead a band through a set — counting in, cueing endings, calling an unplanned tune — and be followed cleanly.

bands.K–2: Say who starts a song in your group performance.
bands.3–5: Practise who leads and who follows in a small group song.
bands.6–8: Assign who leads, cues and counts in for one song, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Assign real stage roles — who leads, who cues, who counts in — for a band performance.
bands.11–12: Lead a real band from a defined role, cueing and counting in, and explain the ear behind each cue.

themes.description: Reading an audience, the dance floor and the listening room; when to talk, when to play, when to stop.
themes.transfer_check: Perform for a live audience and afterwards describe three things you changed in the moment because of what the room did.

bands.K–2: Say if people in the room look happy while you perform.
bands.3–5: Watch an audience and say if they want you to keep playing or stop.
bands.6–8: Read an audience during a short performance and adjust one thing, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Read a real audience during a set and decide when to talk, play or stop.
bands.11–12: Read a real room across a full set and adjust the set list live, defending each call.

themes.theme: The second line and the street
themes.description: Performing outdoors and on the move: the brass band tradition, the parade permit, the crowd, the weather.
themes.transfer_check: Play in a moving or outdoor ensemble for at least twenty minutes, keeping the tune together without amplification.

bands.K–2: Walk in a line while playing or singing, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Perform something outdoors and say what was different from indoors.
bands.6–8: Plan an outdoor performance considering weather and crowd, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Plan a real outdoor performance — the permit, the crowd, the weather — for a brass or street tradition.
bands.11–12: Plan and perform a real street or second-line set, handling weather, permit and crowd on the day.

themes.description: The call, the load-in, the settle-up and the tax form: what a gig actually involves from booking to being paid.
themes.transfer_check: Handle one real or simulated gig end to end — confirmation, load-in list, set, invoice — with every document produced.

bands.K–2: Say what you would want in exchange for playing music for someone.
bands.3–5: List what happens before, during and after a small performance.
bands.6–8: List the steps of a gig from the call to being paid, with a checker.
bands.9–10: List the real steps of a gig — the call, the load-in, the settle-up — and what a tax form asks for.
bands.11–12: Book and complete a real gig end to end, from the call to the settle-up and the tax record.

themes.description: Cables, DI boxes, gain structure and feedback: enough live sound to save your own show.
themes.transfer_check: Set up a small PA for a duo — correct gain structure, no feedback, a monitor mix — and troubleshoot a fault introduced by the assessor.

bands.K–2: Plug in a cable with an adult and say what it does.
bands.3–5: Connect an instrument to an amplifier and check the sound is clean.
bands.6–8: Connect a simple signal chain and identify feedback if it happens, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Connect a real signal chain with a DI box and fix one feedback problem.
bands.11–12: Set up and troubleshoot a real live sound chain, fixing gain and feedback issues under time pressure.

themes.description: The 45-minute set and the 15-minute changeover: preparation, the advance, the stage manager's clock.
themes.transfer_check: Execute a timed festival-style changeover and set under twenty minutes total, meeting a stage manager's schedule.

bands.K–2: Say how fast you would need to set up if your turn was short.
bands.3–5: Time how long it takes to set up and pack up a small performance.
bands.6–8: Plan a set that fits a short changeover time, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Plan a real 45-minute set with a 15-minute changeover, timed and rehearsed.
bands.11–12: Advance and run a real festival slot within its changeover window, coordinating with the stage manager.

themes.description: The shirt, the record, the QR code and the person at the table: selling at the show honestly.
themes.transfer_check: Plan, cost and run a merch table for one show, reconciling stock and cash at the end.

bands.K–2: Make one thing to give away after a performance, with an adult.
bands.3–5: Set up a small table to share something you made after a show.
bands.6–8: Set up a merch table with priced items after a performance, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Set up a real merch table with priced items and a way to pay, honestly.
bands.11–12: Run a real merch table at a show, tracking sales and handling money honestly.

themes.description: Promoter, sound engineer, the contract, the door split and the guarantee: the deal behind the show.
themes.transfer_check: Read a real venue performance agreement, explain its terms in plain words, and negotiate one term with a role-playing promoter.

bands.K–2: Ask a grown-up what a place needs from you before you perform there.
bands.3–5: Find out what a real venue needs before a performance — a time, a sound check.
bands.6–8: Write down what a venue and a performer each agree to before a show, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Write the real deal points between performer and venue — the split, the guarantee.
bands.11–12: Negotiate and document a real venue deal — sound engineer, split, guarantee — before a show.

themes.description: Microphone to preamp to converter to the DAW and back to the speakers: the chain and where it breaks.
themes.transfer_check: Draw the full signal path of a recording setup and trace a silent channel to its fault.

bands.K–2: Say what happens when you speak into a microphone with an adult.
bands.3–5: Trace how sound gets from a microphone to a speaker.
bands.6–8: Trace a signal from microphone to speaker, naming each stage, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Trace a real signal path from mic to preamp to converter to DAW, and find where it breaks.
bands.11–12: Trace and troubleshoot a real signal path end to end, finding and fixing a break in the chain.

themes.description: Dynamic and condenser, polar patterns, placement and the room: the first decision that shapes every recording.
themes.transfer_check: Record the same source with three microphone placements and identify each by ear, explaining the differences.

bands.K–2: Talk close and far from a microphone with an adult and hear the difference.
bands.3–5: Compare how two different microphones sound on the same voice.
bands.6–8: Compare a dynamic and a condenser mic on the same source, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Compare a dynamic and a condenser mic's polar pattern and placement on a real source.
bands.11–12: Choose and place a real microphone for a real source, defending the choice against the room.

themes.description: Takes, the click, punching in and comping: capturing a performance and keeping the best of it.
themes.transfer_check: Track a song in a DAW with a click, punch in a fix, and comp a lead vocal from three takes.

bands.K–2: Try singing a line more than once and pick your favourite with an adult.
bands.3–5: Record two takes of one line and pick the better one.
bands.6–8: Record three takes of one phrase and comp the best parts, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Record several real takes with a click and comp the best performance.
bands.11–12: Track and comp a real performance across multiple takes to a usable final recording.

themes.description: The sound, the performance and the decision: what a producer does that a musician and an engineer don't.
themes.transfer_check: Produce a two-minute recording for another artist — choosing arrangement, take and sound — and explain each decision.

bands.K–2: Say who decides what a recording should sound like overall.
bands.3–5: Say one decision a producer makes that a player does not.
bands.6–8: Name two decisions a producer makes beyond playing or engineering, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Name the decisions a real producer makes about sound and performance in a session.
bands.11–12: Act as producer on a real session, making and defending the sound and performance calls.

themes.description: Timing, tuning and the ethics of it: what to fix, what to leave, and telling the artist.
themes.transfer_check: Edit a tracked performance for timing and tuning, keeping an untouched version, and defend where you stopped.

bands.K–2: Say if a recording should be fixed if a note sounds a little wrong.
bands.3–5: Decide whether to fix or keep a small mistake in a recording.
bands.6–8: Edit one recording, fixing timing or tuning, and say what you left, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Edit a real recording, deciding what to fix, what to leave, and telling the artist why.
bands.11–12: Edit a real take with a clear ethic about what to fix, and explain the choices to the artist.

themes.description: Balance, EQ, compression and space: making twenty tracks into one record.
themes.transfer_check: Mix a multitrack session to a reference, with documented moves, and improve it after a listen on a second system.

bands.K–2: Turn two sounds up and down with an adult until they sound balanced.
bands.3–5: Balance the volume of two tracks so neither drowns the other.
bands.6–8: Balance three tracks and adjust one with EQ, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Balance and EQ several real tracks into one coherent mix.
bands.11–12: Mix a real multi-track recording into a finished balance using EQ, compression and space.

themes.transfer_check: Master a mix to a streaming loudness target and produce correctly formatted files for streaming and CD.

bands.K–2: Say why the same song sounds different on different speakers.
bands.3–5: Listen to one song on two different speakers and say what changed.
bands.6–8: Compare a mix on two playback systems and note one difference, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Compare a real mix across systems and describe what mastering would fix.
bands.11–12: Master a real mix for loudness and translation across formats, and defend the final version.

bands.6–8: Set up a basic home recording spot with one microphone, with a checker.
bands.9–10: Set up a real home studio on a budget — interface, treatment, one good mic.

tracks.name: The industry: rights, money and roles
